blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: State the main reasons for government spending, and follow each through to the effect it intends on the people it serves.

blocks.heading: Goods the market under-provides
blocks.text: Governments spend to provide goods and services that the market left alone tends to under-provide. Public goods such as defence, policing and street lighting over Otavi's taxi rank cannot be confined to those who pay, so private firms tend to build too little of them; merit goods such as schooling and vaccination are under-consumed where households undervalue their benefits when asked to pay directly. In Vietnam, coastal provinces fund sea dykes no single household would raise alone - the same reason, a public good provided by the state.

blocks.heading: Redistribution
blocks.text: Governments also spend to redistribute income. Pensions, child grants and subsidised housing transfer spending power from taxpayers towards households on low incomes, narrowing the gap in living standards that the market alone leaves wide. The grant a Katutura grandmother receives is not payment for a service: it is a deliberate transfer, judged fair because the aim is a floor under the poorest households.

blocks.heading: Spending to steady the economy
blocks.text: Spending is also used to pursue the macroeconomic aims. Where total spending in the economy is weak and workers sit idle, raising government spending tends to raise output and employment where there is spare capacity in the economy; near full capacity, extra spending tends instead to push prices up. Work the chain through an invented project: N$500 million committed to resurfacing the road to Etosha employs road crews, their wages are spent in the towns along the route, and that spending sustains further jobs - one public project raising incomes across the region.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The under-provided goods named here were defined in topic 2.10; the aims this spending pursues are those of topic 4.2.
